flow: Lines 1-7 (Mishnah): Seven days before Yom Kippur the Kohen Gadol is moved from his house to the Parhedrin chamber; a backup priest is prepared in case of disqualification (pesul). Rabbi Yehuda: a backup wife should also be prepared, since 'u'v'ad beito' (Lev 16:6) means 'his wife', and if she dies before Yom Kippur he cannot serve. The Sages reject this: 'if so, there is no end to the matter' (ein la'davar sof - infinite regress).

Lines 8-13 (Gemara opens): Cites the parallel mishna from Parah (tractate Parah 3:1): seven days before the burning of the red heifer (parah adumah), the priest who burns it is likewise separated from his house to the chamber facing the Bira, northeast, called the Stone House (Lishkat Beit HaEven), because all its rites used vessels of dung, stone, and earth.

Lines 14-19: Explains why non-susceptible vessels were required: since a tevul yom (one who immersed that day but before sunset) is valid to burn the parah - contra the Sadducees, who held it must follow sunset after immersion (meorav shemesh) - the Sages would deliberately render the officiating priest tamei and immerse him publicly, to refute the Sadducean position. To prevent that public demonstration from breeding laxity about the parah's purity requirements generally, they mandated vessels immune to tumah (dung/stone/earth).

Lines 20-23: Explains why the chamber was northeast specifically: the parah is classified a chatat (sin-offering; Numbers 19:9,17), and a chatat's slaughter is associated with the north side; Numbers 19:4 requires the sprinkling 'el nokhach penei ohel mo'ed' (toward the front of the Tent of Meeting), i.e. facing east. Northeast satisfies both, and the location itself became a heikher (distinguishing indicator).

Lines 24-26: A short lexical dispute on the word 'bira' from the Parah mishna. Rabbi Yohanan (via Rabbah bar bar Chana): a specific named place on the Temple Mount. Reish Lakish: the term denotes the entire Temple complex, proven from David's phrase in Chronicles ('the bira I have prepared', I Chronicles 29:19); the citation itself (shene'emar ha'bira asher hakhinoti) physically prints on line 27, immediately continuing Reish Lakish's own sentence begun on line 26.

Lines 27-39: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the seven-day separation rule itself. Answer: Leviticus 8:34 (from the milu'im/Tabernacle-inauguration narrative), 'ka'asher asah bayom hazeh tzivah Hashem la'asot lechaper': 'la'asot' (to do) is read as the parah's actions, 'lechaper' (to atone) as Yom Kippur. Neither phrase can cover the whole verse alone (a parah does not atone; and without the gezerah shavah 'la'asot' has no proven referent for Yom Kippur), so the verse must split. A gezerah shavah on the shared word 'tzivah' links Lev 8:34 to Numbers 19:2 (the parah statute), formally proving 'la'asot' refers to the heifer and importing the seven-day sequestration requirement to it. Text is cut off mid-phrase at line 39 ('ve'eima...'), continuing on 2b.

Second, the offerings verse's 'tzavoto' (Num 28:2, 'beyom tzavoto et bnei Yisrael') is rejected because it is a different verb conjugation than 'tzivah', and identical forms are required when available.

Lines 7-10: A challenge from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: they derived a gezerah shavah between 'veshav' and 'uva' (Lev 14:39/44, leprous-house laws) despite those being different verb roots, so why can't 'tzavoto' pair with 'tzivah'? Answer: that method applies only when no identical form is available; here 'tzivah' itself is available in the heifer passage (Num 19), so the identical form must be used.

Lines 11-16: Narrows 'lechaper' (to atone). Could it mean atonement offerings generally? A practical objection (we don't know in advance which kohen serves) is rebutted (the whole mishmeret/beit av rotation is known in advance and could be required to separate) - so the real exclusion is a different principle: we derive a time-fixed matter (the inauguration) from another time-fixed matter (Yom Kippur), excluding daily offerings which recur every day with no fixed annual date.

Lines 16-19: Could it mean Festival service? Excluded because we derive a once-a-year matter from a once-a-year matter; Festivals (Pesach/Sukkot) occur three times a year via their pilgrimage cycle, not once.

Lines 19-23: Could it mean one specific Festival (Chag HaMatzot, since Scripture opens with it first; or Chag HaSukkot, since it has more commandments - sukkah, lulav, water libation)? Excluded structurally: we derive a seven-day separation for a one-day service from a seven-day separation for a one-day service; a Festival's own service spans seven days, so deriving 'seven-for-seven' from 'seven-for-one' is invalid.

Lines 23-28: Could it mean Shemini Atzeret specifically (seven days of Sukkot preceding one culminating day)? Excluded because we derive a case with no sanctity preceding it (the inauguration, ordinary days before) from another case with no preceding sanctity (Yom Kippur); Shemini Atzeret is preceded by seven holy days of Sukkot. A kal va-chomer is proposed (if a case without preceding sanctity needs separation, surely one with preceding sanctity needs it more) and rejected twice: Rav Mesharshiyya ('lo hazeh ketiv, kazeh' - the verse says 'kazeh' [like this], limiting the derivation to cases structurally matching the inauguration, not extending it further by kal va-chomer); Rav Ashi (the primary Festival, Sukkot itself, needs no separation, so its appendage cannot be stricter - and this holds even for the view that Shemini Atzeret is fully independent).

Lines 2-3: Continuation/proof-citation for the tashlumin point (the Sukkah mishna quoted in full).

Lines 4-15: Rabbi Abba excludes Shavuot (Atzeret) via offering profile: Yom Kippur and the inauguration both bring one bull and one ram; Shavuot brings two rams. Challenge: R. Eliezer b. R. Shimon holds Yom Kippur itself has two rams (one from Acharei Mot/Leviticus, one from Pinchas/Numbers) - so what distinguishes it from Shavuot? Resolution: even so, Yom Kippur's two rams serve different functions (one is chovat hayom/day-obligation, the other is mussaf), while Shavuot's two rams (per the Two Loaves verse) are both chovat hayom. The functional mismatch, not mere count, excludes Shavuot.

Lines 16-20: Rabbi Abbahu excludes Rosh Hashana (and re-excludes Shavuot on a second ground) via property source: Yom Kippur's and the inauguration's bull-and-ram both come from the Kohen Gadol's own property ('kach lecha' - take for yourself), while Rosh Hashana's and Shavuot's come from communal funds. This works for the view that 'kach lecha' means personal property; the daf closes mid-word ('ve'aseh...') raising the alternative view, continuing on 3b.
